nodes.label: await inside a loop serialises independent calls
nodes.rationale: Each iteration waits for the previous one, so ten independent 200 ms calls take 2005 ms for no reason. The code is genuinely asynchronous — it releases the thread — it is just needlessly serialised. Async and concurrent are not the same thing, and this is one of the most common .NET performance bugs because it looks completely correct.

nodes.label: Task.WhenAll fan-out
nodes.rationale: Select(...) starts each task; WhenAll launches nothing, it waits for things already in flight. Total time becomes the slowest call rather than the sum — 2005 ms to 204 ms. Beware .Select(async …) over a lazy IEnumerable enumerated twice; .ToArray() before awaiting to fix when the tasks started.

nodes.label: await releases threads rather than creating them
nodes.rationale: await Task.Delay registers a continuation and returns the thread to the pool, so ten in-flight waits cost roughly zero threads — the five observed are just whichever pool threads resumed continuations. Thread.Sleep holds its thread. At 1,000 concurrent requests each waiting 100 ms, blocking needs ~1,000 threads at ~1 MB of stack each; async needs a handful. That difference is the entire value of async on a server.

nodes.label: Throttled fan-out with SemaphoreSlim
nodes.rationale: Unbounded WhenAll over 10,000 items fires 10,000 simultaneous calls and moves your outage to your dependency. Cap it with a SemaphoreSlim, releasing in a finally — an exception that skipped the release permanently shrinks the pool, a slow-motion deadlock that looks like the service getting gradually slower. Measured: 10 checks at concurrency 4 is 3 batches x 200 ms = 603 ms, slower than unbounded on purpose. Parallel.ForEachAsync does the same with less code.

nodes.label: Task.Run is not how you make something async
nodes.rationale: Wrapping a blocking call hides the blocking, it does not remove it, and on a server you now occupy two threads instead of one. Measured at 1,857x slower than the direct call for trivial synchronous work, allocating 1.36 MB. Async has to go all the way down. Task.Run is legitimate only for getting genuinely CPU-bound work off the request thread — and even then a background job may be the better home.

nodes.label: ValueTask on hot synchronous-completion paths
nodes.rationale: async ValueTask always-completed measured at 13.0 µs and zero allocation against async Task's 128.3 µs and 720 KB. It earns its keep on hot paths that usually complete synchronously — a cache hit, a buffered read — but it can only be awaited once, so misusing it is worse than the allocation it saves.

nodes.label: CancellationToken propagation
nodes.rationale: Threading the token through every async method is tedious and is the difference between a client disconnect freeing resources immediately and the server working on answers nobody will read. ASP.NET Core supplies the request's token for free.
